edits.english: MISHNA: In the case of a Jew who sells his wine to a gentile, if he fixed (determined and agreed upon) a price before he measured the wine into the gentile’s vessel, deriving benefit from the money paid for the wine is permitted. He is not considered as one who sells wine used for a libation, as the gentile purchased the wine before it became forbidden, and the money already belonged to the Jew. But if the Jew measured the wine into the gentile’s vessel, and it already became forbidden, before he fixed a price (before the wine was acquired by the gentile), the money paid for the wine is forbidden, because he became like one who sells wine used for a libation, from which benefit is prohibited.

edits.hebrew: המוכר יינו לעובד כוכבים פסק - עמו מעות עד שלא מדד, דמיו מותרין. מפרש בגמרא טעמא: איכא דמוקי לה משום משיכה, בעובד כוכבים קנה. הלכך כשמודד, היינו משיכה וקנייה עובד כוכבים מיד, דהוה ליה לישראל זוזי גבי דעובד כוכבים בהלואה, ויין נסך לא הוי עד דנגע ביה:

edits.english: One who sells his wine to an idol worshipper, if he fixed [the price] - with him, money, before he measured, its money is permitted. The Gemara explains the reason: there are those who establish it based on *meshikha* (pulling/drawing), that an idol worshipper acquires through it. Therefore, when he measures, that is the *meshikha* and the idol worshipper's acquisition immediately, and the Jew has the money from the idol worshipper as a loan, and it does not become libation wine until he touches it.

edits.hebrew: מדד עד שלא פסק דמיו אסורין - דעובד כוכבים לא קנייה במשיכה, דכיון דלא פסק דמיו לא סמכה דעתיה. הלכך כי נגע ביה, הוי יין נסך דישראל. ואיכא דמוקי לה כשהקדים לו עובד כוכבים מעות לישראל, ובגמרא מפרש לה:

edits.english: He measured before he fixed [the price], its money is forbidden - because the idol worshipper did not acquire it through *meshikha*, for since he did not fix the price, his mind was not settled. Therefore, when he touched it, it became libation wine belonging to the Jew. And there are those who establish it as a case where the idol worshipper gave money to the Jew in advance, and the Gemara explains this.

When an Israelite has sold his wine to a gentile, he may benefit from the money received if the wine has not yet been delivered, because the wine is forbidden only from the moment the gentile has touched it, which he could not have done before delivery. But if the gentile took the wine before the final conclusion of the transaction, it is forbidden for the Israelite to benefit from the money received; the gentile having touched the wine before payment, this sale is assimilated to that of wine intended for idols.
GLOSE: As soon as the wine belongs to the gentile, the Israelite no longer has any right to supervise the liquid, and there is reason to fear that the idolater may have touched it. This only concerns the case where the Israelite measured the wine into his own vessel or into the gentile's vessel which has no obstruction. But if the Israelite measured the liquid into the gentile's vessel equipped with a device that can slow down the transfer of wine, or into his own vessel held and agitated by the gentile to facilitate the flow of wine, if the Israelite wants to benefit from the price of his merchandise in this case, he must receive the money before measuring the wine, whether the gentile shakes the vessel left on the ground, or takes it in his hands. However, if the Israelite measured the wine into the vessel belonging to the gentile, and carrying a device that allowed a small part of the liquid first poured by the gentile to be kept in the vessel, a mixture was formed in which the gentile's liquid renders forbidden the wine subsequently poured by the Israelite; however, in a case of accomplished fact, it is permitted to benefit from all the wine poured into the vessel, minus a quantity equal to that of the liquid belonging to the gentile that remained in the receptacle. But, deliberately, the gentile's wine renders the Israelite's wine forbidden when the gentile's liquid is in the vessel itself, but if it is on the rim, whether the vessel is in the gentile's courtyard or in the hands of its owner, or if the Israelite, the wine being in his courtyard, asks the gentile to sell him his vessel, then the wine that the Israelite pours into the vessel is permitted, for it belongs to him as soon as he has touched the liquid on the rim of the receptacle. Likewise, if the gentile, while the Israelite is measuring wine for him, lifted the vessel to show that it belongs to him, the wine is permitted, for the gentile touched it before it was measured: but if the gentile did not lift the vessel containing the wine that the Israelite was to measure, the same law applies to this liquid as to any other wine coming from a gentile. These laws were in force at the time when gentiles offered wine to idols; but as nowadays, there are no more gentiles, it is always permitted to benefit from wine touched by a gentile who does not practice his religion. This is the generally adopted custom and these laws are no longer applied.

One who sells his wine to a non-Jew: if he fixed (determined and agreed upon) the price before he measured the amount of wine sold into the non-Jew's vessels — the money for the wine is permitted, and he is not considered as one who sells libation wine, for the non-Jew purchased the wine before it became forbidden, and the money already belonged to the Jew. But if he measured the wine into the non-Jew's vessels, and it already became forbidden, before he fixed the price, before the wine was acquired by the non-Jew — its money is forbidden, because he became like one who sells libation wine, from which benefit is prohibited.
